title: Competing Offers & Leverage
summary: A real competing offer is the single strongest lever a candidate has. Learn how to sequence interview loops so offers land close together, what to disclose to a recruiter versus keep private, and how much a specific competing number typically moves the needle.

slides.markdown:
A real competing offer changes the shape of a negotiation entirely: instead of asking a company to trust your read of the market, you're handing them a concrete number from a company they actually compete with for talent. Recruiters can act on that far more easily than on cited survey data, because it's a specific, verifiable data point about what it takes to win you.

This topic covers the mechanics of building that leverage deliberately — sequencing multiple interview loops so offers land in the same window, deciding exactly what to disclose to a recruiter versus keep private, and roughly how much a competing number actually moves a real offer. It closes with the sharpest pitfall: bluffing a competing offer that doesn't exist.

slides.sectionTitle: Why a competing offer is the strongest lever
slides.markdown:
Every other form of leverage — market data, scope evidence, enthusiasm — asks a recruiter to take your word (or a third party's) for what you're worth. A competing offer removes that ambiguity: it's a concrete number, from a real company, that already decided to pay it. Recruiters can act on it more directly because retention economics are simple — losing a candidate they've already invested a full loop into is expensive, and matching or beating a real number is often cheaper than restarting the search.

This is also why a competing offer moves a negotiation faster and further than any other lever discussed in this group: a well-evidenced ask without one might move an offer 3-8%, while a real competing offer routinely moves it further, because it changes the recruiter's internal case from "the candidate wants more" to "we will lose this candidate at the current number."

slides.sectionTitle: Sequencing interview timelines so offers land close together
slides.markdown:
Offers rarely arrive in the same week by accident — candidates who end up with real leverage usually engineered the timing deliberately. The core tactic: start your slower-moving, higher-priority companies first, and stagger applications to faster-moving companies so their loops finish around the same time as the slow ones' final rounds.

Concretely, if Company A (your top choice) typically runs a 6-8 week loop and Company B runs a 2-3 week loop, start A immediately and delay starting B by 3-4 weeks, so both plausibly reach final-round or offer stage in the same window. Recruiters at both companies are usually receptive to a direct, honest ask — "I have another process wrapping up around [date], could we target aligning timelines" — since they'd rather accelerate than lose a candidate to a competitor's faster clock.

This requires tracking each company's typical pace from public data (levels.fyi, Blind, Glassdoor interview reviews) and adjusting your own application cadence, not just reacting passively to whatever pace each recruiter sets.

slides.sectionTitle: What to disclose to a recruiter vs. keep private
slides.markdown:
| | Safe / usually helpful to disclose | Risky / usually keep private |
|---|---|---|
| That you have another offer | Yes — this alone is useful leverage and low-risk to share | — |
| The other company's name | Sometimes — can add credibility, but only share if it doesn't hurt you competitively or personally | Avoid if the two companies are direct competitors and disclosure could complicate your standing at either |
| The exact number | Often yes, once you're ready to negotiate seriously — a specific number is what lets a recruiter act | Avoid disclosing before you're sure you want to use it as leverage, since it's hard to walk back once shared |
| Your internal ranking of the offers | No — telling a recruiter they're your backup choice removes your leverage and can affect how hard they fight for you |

The general principle: disclose facts that strengthen your position, withhold anything that weakens it — and remember that once shared, a number or a preference can't be un-shared.

slides.sectionTitle: Using Offer A's number to move Offer B
slides.subTitle: Concrete example
slides.markdown:
```
Situation: Offer A (target company) is $180k base + $60k/yr equity.
Offer B (backup, less preferred) comes in first at $195k base + $40k/yr
equity — a higher base but a less exciting role.

Candidate's message to Offer A's recruiter:
"I wanted to be transparent — I've received another offer at $195k base.
This role is genuinely my top choice, and I'd love to find a way to make
the comp work here. Is there room to move closer to that number, whether
in base or equity?"

Recruiter's typical internal process: takes the specific number to their
comp team or hiring manager, checks what's approvable within policy
(often up to the band max, sometimes an exception above it for a strong
candidate), and returns with a revised offer.

Realistic outcome: Offer A moves to roughly $190k base or an equivalent
equity increase — rarely matches Offer B exactly, since companies
typically don't fully outbid every disclosed number, but moves
substantially closer than the recruiter's original position.
```

The honesty here is doing real work — a specific, real number gives the recruiter something concrete to act on internally, unlike a vague claim of outside interest.

slides.sectionTitle: Disclosing a specific number vs. a range vs. staying silent
slides.subTitle: Compare
slides.markdown:
| | Disclosing the exact number | Disclosing a range | Staying silent on the number |
|---|---|---|---|
| Recruiter's ability to act | Highest — a specific figure is directly actionable | Moderate — gives a target but leaves room to lowball toward the bottom | Lowest — recruiter often can't justify a large move without something concrete |
| Risk to you | If the number is modest, revealing it can cap how far they'll go (why beat a number by much more than necessary) | Balances some leverage with some protection against underbidding | Protects you from an anchor that's too low, but often stalls the negotiation entirely |
| Best used when | Your real number is strong and you want maximum, fast movement | You want leverage without fully exposing your ceiling | Early in a process, before you're ready to negotiate seriously |

Most experienced negotiators default to disclosing the exact number once they're ready to negotiate, because the speed and size of the resulting move usually outweighs the modest risk of capping the ask.

slides.sectionTitle: Bluffing a competing offer that doesn't exist
slides.subTitle: Pitfall
slides.markdown:
Fabricating a competing offer, or inflating a real one's number, is one of the highest-risk moves in the entire negotiation playbook. Recruiters in the same city or industry often know each other, sit on shared Slack communities, and sometimes directly verify claims for senior or high-comp roles — a caught bluff doesn't just fail to move the number, it can rescind the current offer entirely, since it signals the candidate is willing to lie in a professional relationship before even starting.

Even short of outright detection, a bluffed number that's noticeably out of line with market data for your level and location reads as implausible to an experienced recruiter, who negotiates dozens of these conversations a year and has a strong intuition for what's realistic.

The honest alternative is almost always sufficient: a real, even modest, competing offer is still genuine leverage. If you don't have one yet, the tactics from [negotiation tactics and scripts](negotiation-tactics-scripts) — market data, scope evidence, genuine enthusiasm — are a safer and often nearly as effective substitute.

slides.sectionTitle: What happens when timelines don't align naturally
slides.markdown:
Perfect alignment is rare in practice — one loop often runs faster or slower than planned regardless of your sequencing. When a preferred company's offer is still weeks out but a less-preferred one has already landed, the standard move is asking the faster company for a **deadline extension** explicitly to let another process conclude, framed honestly ("I have another loop finishing on [date], could we extend to then").

Most companies will grant a reasonable extension (1-3 weeks is common) for a candidate they genuinely want, since losing a strong candidate over an inflexible date is a worse outcome for them than waiting a bit longer. A company that refuses any extension at all, even a short and reasonably justified one, is itself a data point worth weighing about how that company operates day to day.

Closing, deadlines, and exploding offers covers exactly how to handle a deadline that won't move and what "exploding" offers really mean in practice.

slides.sectionTitle: How much a competing offer typically moves the number
slides.markdown:
There's no universal formula, but a rough pattern experienced negotiators describe: a real, disclosed competing offer typically moves a company's number 5-15% beyond what a well-evidenced ask alone would achieve, and can occasionally trigger a level review if the competing offer clearly implies a higher scope than originally assessed.

Companies rarely match a competing number exactly — doing so can create internal pay-equity problems if it pushes you meaningfully above others at your level — so expect a move that closes most, but not all, of the gap between the two offers. A recruiter coming back with "we can't quite match that, but here's what we can do" is a normal, good-faith outcome, not a sign the leverage failed.

The size of the move also depends heavily on how much the company wants you specifically versus how replaceable your role is perceived to be — leverage is real, but it's not unlimited, and it interacts with how tight the specific hiring market is for your particular skill set.

slides.sectionTitle: When multiple offers reveal a scope, not just a comp, gap
slides.markdown:
The staff-level nuance in this topic: a competing offer isn't only useful for moving comp — it's also a real external calibration of your scope. If two independent companies both leveled you as senior after full loops, and a third offers only mid-level, that's meaningful evidence the third company's leveling assessment may be miscalibrated, not just under-negotiated.

In that situation, the stronger move is often raising the level question directly, citing the pattern ("two other processes have leveled me as senior based on similar scope discussions") rather than only pushing on the number within the lower level's band. [Understanding levels and comp bands](levels-comp-bands) covers why the level itself compounds more than any single negotiated number, which is exactly why this pattern is worth escalating rather than accepting quietly.

slides.sectionTitle: Keeping every process warm while you negotiate
slides.markdown:
A subtle mistake: once you start seriously negotiating with your top-choice company using a competing offer, letting the other process go cold — missing a check-in, delaying a reply — because your attention has shifted. This is risky because negotiations sometimes fail or stall, and a competing offer that quietly expired or was withdrawn in the meantime removes your leverage retroactively without you noticing until it's too late.

The safer practice is treating every live offer as active until you've formally accepted one and declined the others — respond to every recruiter's check-ins on a normal cadence, even the ones you're fairly sure you won't accept, until the negotiation you actually care about is fully resolved.

Once a competing offer has done its job and moved a number, the remaining work shifts from leverage to logistics — handling the deadline the improved offer comes with, deciding what's actually binding versus still negotiable, and formally declining the offers you don't take. Closing, deadlines, and exploding offers picks up exactly there.
